analysis.one_liner: Toughens safety rules, slows slaughterhouse line speeds, and curbs meatpacker market power.
analysis.headline: The bill was sent to five House committees on the day it was introduced, never received a markup or vote, and expired when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have forced OSHA to write new safety standards for meat and poultry plants, funded more inspectors, banned federal approval of faster line speeds unless safety studies cleared them, restricted the no-fault attendance policies that penalize workers for legally protected absences, and let workers sue over safety violations. It would also have restored mandatory country-of-origin labeling for beef, pork, and dairy, and cracked down on packers' market power over ranchers and contract poultry growers. It was referred to five House committees on introduction day and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly half-million meat and poultry processing workers, who have injury and amputation rates well above the private-industry average; livestock ranchers and contract poultry growers, who would gain new antitrust protections and country-of-origin labels; and consumers, who would get origin labels and safer plants.

how_it_helps.text: The bill freezes federal approval of line-speed increases unless an OSHA-led inspection certifies the faster pace would not harm worker safety, and bars the Agriculture Secretary from spending funds on any policy that speeds lines during the covered period [S3].

It appropriates $60 million a year from FY2022 through FY2027 to hire additional OSHA inspectors, and requires a permanent regional inspection program targeting amputation hazards, ergonomics, line speeds, bathroom access, chemical exposure, and extreme temperatures [S2] [S3].

It makes it an unlawful employment practice for an employer to run a no-fault attendance policy that does not clearly exempt legally protected leave, and gives workers the FMLA's court remedies and civil penalties [S2] [S3].

It requires OSHA to issue an emergency temporary standard against workplace COVID-19 exposure within seven days, ergonomic and medical-referral standards for meat and poultry plants, verifiable toilet-access rights, and a private right of action allowing workers to sue for safety violations with compensatory and punitive damages [S2] [S3].

It restores mandatory country-of-origin labeling for beef and pork and extends it to dairy products, and amends the Packers and Stockyards Act to bar forward contracts without firm base prices, restrict packer ownership and feeding of livestock, police the poultry tournament pay system, and require grant recipients to sign labor peace agreements and stay out of large packers' hands for ten years [S2] [S3].

It adds $100 million for meat and poultry processing grants through FY2031 and expands the Local Agriculture Market Program, and directs GAO to study food-system fragility, racial disparities in processing, and line speeds [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Meat and poultry processing companies, which would bear slower line speeds, new OSHA standards, weekly pandemic reporting, and litigation exposure; large packers, whose contracting and livestock-ownership practices would be restricted; and retailers and importers, who would absorb country-of-origin labeling costs.

drawbacks.text: The attendance-policy subtitle applies to virtually every employer covered by Title VII, not just meatpacking plants, so it imposes new paperwork, disclosure, and litigation obligations across the economy [S3].

Mandatory country-of-origin labeling was previously struck down after World Trade Organization disputes in which Canada and Mexico won retaliation rights, so its costs and trade consequences were a serious objection [S3].
The bill requires several OSHA standards on fixed statutory deadlines, including an emergency COVID standard within seven days, a pace that would curtail the usual notice-and-comment process [S3].

Freezing line speeds and adding inspection, reporting, and labeling requirements would raise processing costs that could be passed to consumers, and the private right of action invites litigation against plants beyond what existing enforcement provides [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The worker-safety case is strong: the bill's own findings document injury, amputation, and musculoskeletal rates far above average, pandemic conditions that prioritized processing over health, and abusive attendance discipline [S3]. The costs fall on a profitable, highly concentrated industry and partly on consumers, though the broad attendance-policy reach and rushed rulemaking deadlines were genuine design flaws. On balance the bill traded throughput and compliance costs for enforceable safety protections, and the side that avoided paying was the industry the rules were aimed at [S2] [S3].

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to five House committees on the day it was introduced, then to a House Agriculture subcommittee in January 2022, and no committee ever held a markup or brought it to a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ro Khanna introduced the bill on December 13, 2021, and it was referred the same day to the Committees on Agriculture, Education and Labor, Oversight and Reform, House Administration, and Judiciary [S1] [S5].

On January 4, 2022 it was referred to the House Agriculture Subcommittee on Livestock and Foreign Agriculture, and the action history records no further steps — no markup, no vote, no floor action — before the 117th Congress expired on January 3, 2023 [S5] [S1].
The bill attracted only four cosponsors, all House Democrats, and no Senate companion appears in the record [S4].

The CRS summary describes the bill as funding OSHA inspectors through FY2027, restricting no-fault attendance policies, expanding safety requirements for meat and poultry plants, funding processing grants through FY2031, and requiring country-of-origin labeling of beef, pork, and dairy [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Meat and poultry processing companies and large packers avoided the line-speed limits, OSHA standards, attendance-policy restrictions, antitrust constraints, and litigation exposure the bill would have imposed; meatpacking workers, ranchers, and poultry growers received none of the protections.

against.what_they_did: Received the bill on introduction day and never held a markup or vote; its Livestock and Foreign Agriculture Subcommittee took the referral on January 4, 2022 and recorded no further action.

against.name: Meat and poultry processing industry trade associations
against.what_they_did: Opposed line-speed limits, mandatory country-of-origin labeling, and expanded OSHA enforcement of the kind this bill proposed.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call exists; its support was entirely Democratic — one sponsor and four Democratic cosponsors, with no Republican backing and no Senate companion in the record [S4].

industries.note: The bill would have frozen line-speed increases, required ergonomic and infectious-disease OSHA standards, mandated weekly pandemic reporting, restricted attendance-point discipline, and given workers a private right of action — each a direct hit to plant throughput, flexibility, and litigation exposure [S2] [S3]. Workers' gains in this bill come at these companies' expense, which is why the industry's interest runs against the public's here.

industries.industry: Large livestock packers with concentrated market share
industries.note: The bill bars forward contracts without firm base prices, restricts packer ownership and feeding of livestock, polices the poultry tournament pay system, limits spot-market purchases, and bars processing-grant recipients from selling to packers holding more than 10 percent market share for ten years [S3]. These provisions would unwind practices that concentrate the industry, and the bill's gains to ranchers and growers come directly out of packers' pricing power.

industries.industry: Livestock ranchers and contract poultry growers
industries.note: Ranchers and growers would get restored country-of-origin labeling, a right to pay data used to set their compensation, protection from retaliatory contract termination, and attorney-fee awards — ordinary farming families whose interest aligns with consumers wanting origin labels [S3].

industries.industry: Beef and pork importers and meat retailers
industries.note: Mandatory origin labeling for beef, pork, and dairy would impose new compliance costs on retailers and could disadvantage imported meat at the shelf; consumers gain the labeling information the costs buy [S3].
